title: The cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis
blurb: Order the cell cycle and the stages of mitosis, contrast mitosis with meiosis, and explain where genetic variation and nondisjunction come from.
question: A skin cell and a cell in the ovary both start with 46 chromosomes. One divides to repair a cut, the other to make eggs. How many cells does each division produce, how many chromosomes does each new cell carry, and why are the egg cells all genetically different?

teach.body: Formal definition: the cell cycle is the ordered series of events by which a cell grows, copies its DNA and divides. Most of it is interphase: G1 (growth and normal function), S (DNA replication) and G2 (growth and preparation for division). Then comes mitosis and cytokinesis. Plain English: a cell spends most of its life working and getting ready, copies its instruction book once, then splits. Checkpoints control each step; losing that control leads to cancer.

teach.h: One turn of the cell cycle
teach.caption: After S phase each chromosome is two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

steps.label: Prophase
steps.sub: Chromosomes condense; spindle forms; envelope breaks down

steps.label: Metaphase
steps.sub: Chromosomes line up at the cell equator

steps.label: Anaphase
steps.sub: Sister chromatids separate to opposite poles

teach.caption: Result: 2 genetically identical diploid daughter cells (46 to 46 in humans) for growth, repair and replacement.

The panels are shuffled, but the numbers run in stage order: follow 1 to 5 around the figure. Note the chromosomes lined up across the middle in metaphase, pulled to opposite poles in anaphase, and the pinching cell of telophase.

items.label: chromosomes in a body (somatic) cell: diploid, 2n
22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes
chromosomes in a gamete (egg or sperm): haploid, n

teach.caption: Sex chromosomes: XX female, XY male. A karyotype is a picture of an individual's chromosomes arranged in pairs.

teach.h: Meiosis: two divisions, half the chromosomes
teach.body: Meiosis makes gametes in the testes and ovaries. DNA is replicated once, then the cell divides twice. Meiosis I is the reduction division: in prophase I homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis, forming tetrads) and swap segments (crossing over); in metaphase I the pairs line up and sort independently; in anaphase I the homologs separate. Meiosis II works like mitosis: sister chromatids separate. Result: 4 genetically different haploid cells (46 to 23).

teach.caption: Variation in meiosis comes from crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization (plus mutation).

head: Condition
Karyotype
Chromosomes
teach.caption: Nondisjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate in meiosis, giving gametes with an abnormal number (aneuploidy).

teach.h: Worked scenario: Lena's onion root tip
teach.body: Lena, a nursing applicant, studies dividing onion root tip cells. Cell 1 shows chromosomes lined up across the middle: metaphase. Cell 2 shows chromatids being pulled to opposite ends: anaphase. Cell 3 shows a new wall forming between two nuclei: cytokinesis by a cell plate, because plant cells cannot pinch in like animal cells. Root tips grow by mitosis, so every new cell keeps the full diploid chromosome number.

teach.text: Anaphase I separates HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes; sister chromatids separate in anaphase II and in mitotic anaphase. Crossing over happens in prophase I only (not mitosis, not prophase II). DNA replicates in S phase, not prophase. Mitosis makes 2 diploid cells, not 4 haploid ones. Humans have 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs, not 46 pairs.

items: Interphase = G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (prep). Lost checkpoint control can lead to cancer.
Mitosis PMAT: prophase, metaphase (line up), anaphase (sisters separate), telophase; then cytokinesis.
Mitosis: 1 division, 2 identical diploid cells. Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 different haploid cells.
Prophase I: synapsis and crossing over. Anaphase I: homologs separate. Anaphase II: sisters separate.

summary: You can now order the cell cycle and the stages of mitosis, compare mitosis with meiosis by divisions, cell number, chromosome number and genetic identity, and explain how crossing over and independent assortment create variation. You can also link nondisjunction to trisomy 21, Turner and Klinefelter syndromes.

A.q: During which phase of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
A.why: DNA is copied during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids before mitosis starts.

whyNot.1: In prophase the already-copied chromosomes condense; replication happened earlier, in S phase.
whyNot.2: G2 is growth and preparation for division after replication is complete.
whyNot.3: In anaphase the copies are separated, not made.

A.q: In which stage of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell?
A.why: In anaphase the centromeres split and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles.

whyNot.0: In metaphase the chromosomes line up at the metaphase plate; they have not separated yet.
whyNot.2: In telophase the separated chromosomes are already at the poles and nuclear envelopes re-form.
whyNot.3: In prophase chromatin condenses and the spindle forms; chromatids are still joined.

A.q: A human skin cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. What does the division produce?
options: Two identical cells with 23 chromosomes each
Four varied cells with 23 chromosomes each
Two identical cells with 46 chromosomes each
Four identical cells with 46 chromosomes each
A.why: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells, so 46 chromosomes become 46 in each cell.

whyNot.0: Mitosis does not halve the chromosome number; halving happens in meiosis.
whyNot.1: Four genetically different haploid cells is the outcome of meiosis.
whyNot.3: Mitosis is a single division, so it produces two cells, not four.

B.q: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes takes place during:
B.why: In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) and exchange segments: crossing over.

whyNot.0: Homologs are no longer paired in meiosis II, so crossing over cannot occur in prophase II.
whyNot.1: Homologous chromosomes do not pair in mitosis, so there is no crossing over.
whyNot.2: In anaphase I the homologs separate; crossing over has already happened.

B.q: Which event occurs in anaphase I of meiosis but NOT in anaphase of mitosis?
B.why: Anaphase I is unique in separating homologous chromosomes; the sister chromatids stay together until meiosis II.

whyNot.1: Sister chromatids separate in mitotic anaphase (and anaphase II), not in anaphase I.
whyNot.2: Spindle fibers pull chromosomes in both mitosis and meiosis.
whyNot.3: Chromosomes move to opposite poles in every anaphase.

B.q: A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21. Which process most likely caused this?
B.why: Nondisjunction (chromosomes failing to separate in meiosis) gives a gamete with an extra chromosome 21: trisomy 21, Down syndrome.

whyNot.0: Crossing over swaps segments between homologs; it does not change the chromosome number.
whyNot.2: A frameshift changes the base sequence of a gene, not the number of chromosomes.
whyNot.3: Normal S-phase replication copies each chromosome once and does not create an extra chromosome.

C.q: Which statement correctly compares mitosis and meiosis?
options: Both produce four genetically different cells
Mitosis halves the chromosome number of cells
Homologs pair up in meiosis but not mitosis
Meiosis repairs damaged somatic body tissue
C.why: Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) in prophase I of meiosis; they never pair in mitosis.

whyNot.0: Mitosis produces two genetically identical cells; only meiosis produces four different cells.
whyNot.1: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number (2n to 2n); meiosis halves it.
whyNot.3: Tissue repair is the job of mitosis; meiosis makes gametes in the gonads.

C.q: An organism has a diploid number of 2n = 16. After meiosis of one parent cell, how many chromosomes are in each gamete, and how many cells result?
C.why: Meiosis halves the number (2n = 16 to n = 8) and its two divisions produce 4 cells.

whyNot.0: 16 chromosomes in 2 cells is the outcome of mitosis, not meiosis.
whyNot.1: The chromosome number is right, but two divisions produce 4 cells, not 2.
whyNot.2: Gametes are haploid, so they carry 8 chromosomes, not 16.

C.q: In an onion root tip, one cell shows chromosomes lined up along the cell's center and another shows a new wall forming between two nuclei. Which stages are shown?
C.why: Chromosomes at the equator means metaphase; plant cells divide their cytoplasm by building a cell plate.

whyNot.1: In anaphase chromatids are moving apart, and plant cells do not form a cleavage furrow.
whyNot.2: Metaphase is right, but a cleavage furrow is how animal cells divide; plants form a cell plate.
whyNot.3: In prophase chromosomes are condensing, not lined up at the center.

reteach.title: Photocopying vs shuffling a deck
reteach.question: Imagine copying a recipe book on a photocopier versus dealing half a shuffled deck of cards to each player. Which is mitosis and which is meiosis?

blocks.body: Mitosis is the photocopier: you copy the whole book (S phase), then hand one complete, identical copy to each of two people. Meiosis is the card dealer: you double the deck, swap a few cards between matching pairs (crossing over), shuffle how the pairs are split (independent assortment), then deal it out twice so four players each get half a deck, and no two hands are the same.

blocks.text: The card swap (crossing over) only happens in the first deal: prophase I, never in mitosis.

explain.body: Most of the cell cycle. G1: the cell grows and does its normal job. S: DNA replicates, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. G2: more growth and preparation for division.

test.q: A cell has just completed S phase. Each of its chromosomes now consists of:
options: Two sister chromatids at a centromere
Two homologous chromosomes joined in synapsis
test.why: S phase replicates the DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

whyNot.0: A single chromatid describes a chromosome before S phase (in G1).
whyNot.2: Synapsis of homologs happens in prophase I of meiosis, not as a result of S phase.
whyNot.3: Tetrads form when homologs pair in prophase I; one replicated chromosome has two chromatids.

explain.body: PMAT. Prophase: condense, spindle forms, envelope breaks down. Metaphase: line up at the equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate. Telophase: nuclei re-form. Cytokinesis: furrow (animal) or cell plate (plant).

test.q: Which order of the stages of mitosis is correct?
test.why: PMAT: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, followed by cytokinesis.

whyNot.0: Chromosomes must line up (metaphase) before they are pulled apart (anaphase).
whyNot.1: Prophase comes first, because chromosomes must condense before they can line up.
whyNot.3: Chromatids separate (anaphase) before nuclear envelopes re-form (telophase).

explain.body: One replication, two divisions. Meiosis I: homologs pair and cross over (prophase I), pairs line up independently (metaphase I), homologs separate (anaphase I). Meiosis II: sister chromatids separate. Four haploid, genetically different cells.

test.q: Which pair of events are sources of genetic variation during meiosis?
options: Binary fission and crossing over in mitosis
test.why: Crossing over (prophase I) and independent assortment (metaphase I) shuffle alleles, so every gamete is different.

whyNot.0: Binary fission is prokaryotic division, and crossing over does not occur in mitosis.
whyNot.1: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and replication copies DNA faithfully; neither shuffles alleles.
whyNot.2: Replication and spindle formation happen in every division and do not create new combinations.

explain.body: Humans: 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs (22 autosome pairs + XX or XY). Body cells are diploid (2n), gametes haploid (n = 23). If chromosomes fail to separate (nondisjunction), a gamete gets one too many or too few.

test.q: Turner syndrome results from nondisjunction. Which karyotype does it produce?
test.why: Turner syndrome is 45,X: one sex chromosome is missing.

whyNot.1: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, which has an extra X.
whyNot.2: Trisomy 21 (an extra chromosome 21) is Down syndrome.
whyNot.3: 46,XY is a typical male karyotype, not a nondisjunction disorder.
